title: Re-covering a footstool lid with foam and fabric
subtitle: Remove the old fabric and foam from a storage footstool lid, cut and fit new foam, and staple on a new fabric cover with neatly folded corners
excerpt: How to re-cover a storage footstool lid. Covers removing the old fabric and foam, cutting and fitting new upholstery foam, wrapping with wadding, and stapling the new fabric cover with mitred corners.
sourceNotes: UK upholstery trade practice. City and Guilds upholstery syllabi (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A CMHR (combustion-modified high-resilience) foam block cut to the size of the footstool lid. Medium-firm density (36 oz) at 50 mm thickness gives a comfortable sit-on surface. UK regulations require CMHR foam in any domestic upholstered furniture.

The method of folding the fabric at the corner of a seat or lid so that the fold lies flat and neat. The standard approach is to fold one side in first, cut away the excess at the corner point, then fold the adjacent side over. A clean corner fold is the mark of careful upholstery work.

content.text: A storage footstool has a flat, padded lid:
glued to a plywood base, wrapped in wadding, and covered with fabric. The re-cover job is: remove, replace foam and fabric, staple back. The
are the skill. Everything else is cutting and stapling.

Wear protective gloves and a dust mask when stripping old foam. Pre-1988 foam may contain brominated flame-retardants. Work outdoors or in a well-ventilated space. Bag the stripped foam in a sealed bag for disposal.
Strip the old cover and foam

Remove the lid from the footstool body. Use the staple remover to lift all the staples from the underside of the lid base. Peel off the old fabric and wadding. Cut the old foam away from the plywood base; if it is glued, a sharp utility knife scores and lifts it in sections. Sand off any adhesive residue.
Cut and fit the new foam

Cut the new foam to the same dimensions as the plywood base. A 50 mm medium-firm CMHR foam is right for a footstool lid. Cut with a sharp utility knife against a straight edge, or use the upholstery shears for thinner foam. Glue the foam to the top of the plywood with spray adhesive or a thin bead of PVA around the perimeter. Allow to tack before placing the foam.
Wrap with wadding and cut the fabric

Wrap the foam in a layer of upholstery wadding (polyester Dacron wrap), pulling it over the edges and stapling to the underside. Cut the fabric 100 mm larger than the lid in both directions. Centre the fabric over the wadded lid face-down on a clean surface.

Starting at the centre of one long edge, pull the fabric firmly over the edge and place a staple every 50 mm along that side. Work to the other side and repeat, pulling evenly. Do the short sides next. At each corner, cut a triangle of excess fabric close to the corner point. Fold one side's overlap in tight to the corner, then fold the adjacent side over to form a neat diagonal fold. Staple both down firmly. The fold should look like a wrapped present corner: flat and sharp.

attrs.symptom: The fabric pulls or puckers at the corners
attrs.cause: Too much excess fabric at the corner point, or the fabric was not pulled evenly before stapling.
attrs.fix: Remove the corner staples, re-cut the excess closer to the fold line, and re-staple while pulling the fabric evenly in both directions.

attrs.symptom: The foam lifts or moves under the fabric after a few uses
attrs.cause: The foam was not glued down before covering.
attrs.fix: Remove the fabric, lift the foam, apply spray adhesive or PVA to the base, re-set the foam, allow to tack, then re-cover.
